G2672.origine: The word comes from the Greek κατάρα (curse) with the verbal suffix -άομαι. It generally translates the Hebrew קָלַל (qalal, to lighten, to dishonor, to treat with contempt). The root carries the idea of pronouncing destructive words: to curse is to unleash the destructive power of the word. Biblical cursing is not a mere insult, but a word that engages a spiritual reality.
G2672.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament. Jesus speaks of it twice: he commands his disciples to bless those who curse them (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28), overturning the ethics of the world. Mark reports that Jesus cursed the barren fig tree, which immediately withered (Mark 11:21), demonstrating the power of the curse pronounced by Jesus. Paul and James revisit the use of words: we should not curse those who persecute us (Romans 12:14), and it is absurd to bless God while cursing men created in His image (James 3:9). Finally, Matthew 25:41 describes the cursed at the final judgment, a state to which Jesus consigns the reprobate.
G2672.portee: This word teaches the power of the human word: to bless or to curse is not trivial; it engages our will and our relationship with God. Jesus calls Christians to break with cursing and to bless their enemies, which is a mark of spiritual transformation. For the Christian, it is a call to master their tongue and to let God alone judge, rather than to take revenge through words.

sens: to render useless, ineffective
to abolish, repeal a law or order
to destroy, annihilate
to strip of power or authority
to be freed from, to be released from
G2673.detail:
1. To render something inactive or unproductive: this is the primary idea of the word, which evokes a field where a tree does not bear fruit and "occupies uselessly" the land (Luke 13:7).
2. To abolish, repeal a law, a covenant, or an order: this is the legal sense, when one cancels what had the force of law. The grace of God does not destroy the law (Romans 3:31), but it changes its scope.
3. To annihilate, to completely destroy something: when God will destroy food and the stomach, or when the Lord will destroy all dominion (1 Corinthians 6:13 and 15:24).
4. To remove the strength, effectiveness, or power from something: death, for example, will be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26), the Antichrist will be destroyed (2 Thessalonians 2:8).
5. To be freed from an obligation or a bond: a woman whose husband has died is released from the law of marriage (Romans 7:2), one can be freed from the law (Romans 7:6).
G2673.origine: The word comes from the Greek "kata" (against, down) combined with "argos" (inactive, idle), hence the primary meaning "to render inactive." It is a causative formation: it does not merely state that something becomes useless, but that one renders it useless, depriving it of its effectiveness. In the Greek texts of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew "betal" which means to cease, to annul. The word family includes "argos" (idle, inactive) and other compounds with "kata" that mark an action that goes against something, that fails or annuls it.
G2673.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians). It takes nuanced meanings depending on the context: in the concrete sense in Luke 13:7 (the useless tree), in the legal sense in Romans (the law, the covenant) and Galatians (circumcision), in the eschatological sense in 1 Corinthians 15 (death, powers). In the passive voice, it often means "to be annulled, to become ineffective" or, with the preposition "apo", "to be separated from, freed from." The word is often used to express the abolition of what was old by the establishment of the new: the old law by the covenant in Christ, death by resurrection.
G2673.portee: This word shows the transformative power of the Gospel: it does not simply add; it annuls, brings down, renders ineffective everything that opposed God or limited His plan. For the believer, it speaks of liberation from old obligations (the law of sin, the bondage of doubt) through the efficacy of the cross and resurrection. It is also a promise: the powers of evil, death itself, will ultimately be annihilated. This verb invites recognition that only God has the power to end things and render obsolete the lies and authorities contrary to His reign.

sens: to place someone in a category or group
to assign someone a place alongside others
G2674.detail:
1. The word expresses the action of placing someone in a set, enumerating them among the members of a group. In Acts 1:17, it is said that Judas was "counted among" the apostles: he was listed among them, he had his place among them.
2. It is to recognize someone with a status, a belonging: the text immediately adds that he "had part in the same ministry," which shows that "to count among" also means to grant him a place and responsibilities in the community.
G2674.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "arithmeō" (to count, to enumerate) preceded by the prefix "kata" (downward, completely). This composition suggests an exhaustive counting or a methodical enumeration. The word translates in ancient Greek the Hebrew "hichassab" (Chronicles 31:19), which belongs to the same family as "hasab": to make a count, to enumerate.
G2674.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:17, in the context of replacing Judas after the Ascension. Peter speaks of Judas who was "counted among" the twelve apostles and who shared their ministry, although he later betrayed them. This passage shows that "to count among" describes an official belonging to a group, with the rights and duties that this implies.
G2674.portee: This word reminds us that belonging to the community of apostles — and more broadly to the Church — is not a vague or informal status. To be "counted among" the disciples is to have a real place, responsibilities, and shared resources with others. For the reader, it is an invitation to take seriously their inscription in the people of God.

sens: To repair, mend (a damaged object)
To constitute, assemble the elements of something to make it complete
To prepare, equip someone or something for a purpose
To perfect, bring to moral or spiritual fulfillment
G2675.detail:
1. To repair, mend: this is primarily a manual task, that of restoring what is damaged or worn. The disciples Peter and John "were mending their nets" (Matthew 4:21; Mark 1:19), meaning they were sewing up the tears so that they could be used again for fishing.
2. To constitute, assemble: the word means to gather the appropriate elements so that something is whole and ready. When it is said that "the world was formed by the word of God" (Hebrews 11:3), it means that God assembled and organized all the parts of the universe to make a coherent whole.
3. To prepare, equip: this involves putting someone in a position to do something, providing them with what they lack. Paul wants to "complete what is lacking in your faith" by visiting the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 3:10), meaning to give them what will enable them to be full and mature.
4. To perfect, bring to fulfillment: in a spiritual or moral sense, it is to lead someone or something to the end of its formation, to excellence. To be "perfectly united" in the same mind (2 Corinthians 13:11) or to be "equipped in every good thing" (Hebrews 13:21) means to reach complete maturity and deep harmony.
G2675.origine: The word is composed of κατά ("according to", "completely") and the root ἄρτ- (which evokes adjustment, suitability, what is "just"). The ancient Greek verb ἀρτιάω meant "to make complete, perfect". In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew כּוּן ("to establish, to set up") and כְּלַל ("to accomplish, to complete"), which shows that the biblical idea is one of solidity and total fulfillment.
G2675.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Hebrews, 1 Peter). Its meaning varies according to the context: in a concrete sense, it refers to the mending of nets (Matthew 4:21; Mark 1:19); in a cosmic sense, it speaks of the formation of the world (Hebrews 11:3) or the creation of a judgment army (Romans 9:22); in a spiritual and ethical sense, it applies to brotherly correction (Galatians 6:1, where it means "to restore"), to the growth of faith (1 Thessalonians 3:10), and to the perfection of the Church in love and unity (2 Corinthians 13:11; Hebrews 13:21). The tone progresses from physical repair to lasting spiritual growth.
G2675.portee: This word teaches that Christian perfection is not an impossible demand or an abstract virtue, but a work of formation, like that of a fisherman mending his nets. It involves both an action of God who "forms" (Hebrews 11:3) and human collaboration ("be perfect"). The believer is never "finished": they are a being in formation, constantly called to spiritual fulfillment in the life of the Church and in brotherly correction.

sens: Action of making something complete and well-adjusted, without defect
Moral or spiritual strengthening of a person
Fulfillment of what is lacking to achieve excellence
G2676.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of putting in place or completing something so that it functions perfectly, like adjusting the parts of a whole — an image drawn from the work of artisans (2 Corinthians 13:9 speaks of the perfection of the Corinthians, what is lacking in their faith and communal life).
2. In the spiritual and moral realm, it signifies the inner strengthening of a person, their firm establishment in virtue and Christian maturity — it is not an instant perfection, but a work of growth.
3. The term also encompasses the idea of filling gaps, completing what is unfinished, so that the Church or the believer reaches their full stature in Christ.
G2676.origine: This word comes from the verb κατα-ρτίζω (katartizô), which literally means "to assemble" or "to put in order": κατά ("according to") + ἀρτίζω ("to adapt, arrange"). The root evokes the image of the carpenter or fisherman preparing their nets, placing each element in its proper place. In Hebrew, this order and completeness are related to the idea of שׁלום (shalom), the peace that comes from wholeness.
G2676.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 13:9. Paul asks in his prayer that the Corinthians experience "perfection", meaning that they strengthen their church life and fill the gaps in their faith. Here, the word denotes the spiritual goal toward which all of Paul's exhortation to the Corinthians is directed: a growth in holiness and Christian unity, far from any complacency or slackness.
G2676.portee: This word reminds Christians that it is not about a fixed perfection, but a continual growth where God himself strengthens and completes what is lacking. It invites everyone to recognize their shortcomings and to desire spiritual strengthening, not out of vanity, but as an essential part of church life where the saints build each other up.

sens: Action of making someone or something complete, finished, and capable of its function
Spiritual maturation of believers towards fullness in Christ
Preparation and equipping to accomplish a service
State of what is well-adjusted, in good order and functional
G2677.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of making something complete and operational, like equipment that is adjusted or a body made fit to function. It is the process that leads to the intended end, to fulfillment.
2. In the biblical context, it is primarily the spiritual work by which God and His Church make believers complete, mature, and functional in their faith. In Ephesians 4:12, Paul speaks of the "perfection of the saints": it is the spiritual growth of Christians that is built up through various gifts and ministries.
3. Perfection is inseparable from a mission: one is perfected only for a purpose. The saints are perfected "for the work of ministry and for the edification of the body of Christ" — it is a growth oriented towards service and the building up of the Church.
4. The image is one of harmony and balance: when everything is well-adjusted, when each element is in its place and performs its function, the whole operates. It is this state of order and efficiency that the word denotes.
G2677.origine: The word comes from the verb κατάρτιζω (katartizô), which means "to adjust", "to put in order", "to make complete". The root evokes the idea of preparing something, arranging it so that it is fit for its function: one adjusts a sail, arranges the elements of a whole. The noun κατάρτισμός names this result, this state of what is well-prepared and completed. It is the same reality as κατάρτισις, another nominal form of the same verb.
G2677.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 4:12. Paul uses it in his teaching on the spiritual gifts given to the Church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers have received their gifts precisely for the "perfection of the saints". This is not a static state, but a dynamic process by which the Church grows towards its maturity. The use emphasizes that the growth of Christians individually is inseparable from the edification of the entire body of Christ. Thus, perfection is both personal (each saint progresses) and communal (the body of Christ is built up).
G2677.portee: For today's Christian, this word reminds us that spiritual growth is not a private accumulation of knowledge, but a progressive equipping for service. Every gift received from Christ, every ministry, every step of maturation has a purpose: to make both individual believers and the entire Church more capable. It is an invitation to see one's own progression in Christ as inseparable from one's contribution to the edification of the Church.

sens: Make a hand gesture to attract attention or command silence
Give a signal by raising or waving the hand
Command or order by gesture without speaking
G2678.detail:
1. Make a hand gesture to attract attention or command silence. It is the image of a hand waving or raised to say "listen to me" or "be quiet." Peter in prison makes a "sign" with his hand to his companions to silence them and listen to him (Acts 12:17), and Paul uses this same gesture before speaking to a tumultuous crowd (Acts 13:16, Acts 21:40).
2. Give a signal by raising or waving the hand. The gesture replaces speech and speaks to everyone at once, particularly useful when there is noise or a crowd needs to be calmed. Alexander, pushed forward by the crowd in Ephesus, "makes a sign" with his hand to the tumultuous people in order to speak (Acts 19:33).
3. Command or order by gesture without speaking. It is a gesture of authority: the one who makes a hand signal imposes silence and takes control of the situation. All four uses in Acts show men who have something important to say and who first impose silence with this gesture.
G2678.origine: The word is composed of "kata" ("downward") and "seiō" ("to shake, to wave"). The basic image is that of a hand waving or lowering as if to command. This verb appears only in Acts in the Greek New Testament, but the Greek Old Testament also knows it. The root "seiō" is found in "seismic" in French: something that shakes and trembles.
G2678.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Acts of the Apostles, always in the sense of "make a hand signal." Each time, it involves a leader or speaker (Peter, Paul, Alexander) who must speak before a crowd and begins by imposing silence with this gesture. It is a natural rhetorical device: before speaking, one captures attention. The gesture is always effective—it produces "a deep silence" (Acts 21:40)—which shows that it is a universally understood signal. The use of the word emphasizes the contrast between the tumult and the speech that follows.
G2678.portee: This word reminds us that speech is not isolated: it is accompanied by a visible presence and intention. Peter and Paul, before preaching or testifying, first seek to be heard. It is a lesson in communication and humility: the one who has an important word to share begins by honoring their audience by asking them to listen. The silence obtained by this simple gesture also shows that a free action of the faithful is more powerful than any noise.

sens: Completely destroy, knock down structures
Ruin, lay waste
Destroy someone's work or altars
G2679.detail:
1. The word primarily means to physically destroy, to knock down what has been built: one thinks of a building being dismantled stone by stone. In Acts 15:16, it refers to the "tent of David" that has been overthrown, destroyed, and which God promises to restore—the image is that of a collapsed structure that will be rebuilt.
2. More broadly, it means to lay waste, to annihilate. This is why the translation "ruins" is appropriate in Acts 15:16 to describe the state of destruction in which the tent of David finds itself.
3. Finally, the word can mean to destroy what belongs to someone, particularly their altars and temples. In Romans 11:3, Paul cites a psalm where adversaries have "overthrown" the altars of the Lord, meaning they have destroyed them to annihilate the worship of Israel.
G2679.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "kata-" (downward, completely) and "skaptō" (to dig, to excavate). The basic image is thus that of "digging down," but it evolves towards the meaning of "demolishing" and "destroying." In Acts and Romans, it translates Hebrew words that mean "to break," "to overthrow," "to demolish"—strong verbs that describe the systematic destruction of a work or institution.
G2679.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 15:16, it describes the destruction of the tent of David, a symbol of the reign and promise to David—destruction that God promises to repair. In Romans 11:3, it denotes the hostile action of enemies who have destroyed the altars of the Lord to persecute Israel. In both cases, it is an act of radical destruction, either by God's enemies or in the history of the chosen people. The context is always one of rupture, dismantling, followed (in Acts) by divine restoration.
G2679.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and judges the destruction of His work and the worship due to Him. But more profoundly, Acts 15:16 teaches that God does not leave His promises in ruins: He raises up, restores, rebuilds. This is a reason for hope for the believer when God's plan seems annihilated by circumstances.

sens: Set up, assemble the elements of a building or structure
Arrange in advance, make ready, put in order
Smooth the way, make it accessible by removing obstacles
G2680.detail:
1. The word first denotes the action of constructing or assembling: erecting a house (Hebrews 3:3-4), a tent of worship (Hebrews 9:2), an ark (Hebrews 11:7). It conveys the idea of giving form, structuring, putting together the material elements.
2. It also means to prepare in the sense of making ready, arranging for use: preparing a people for the Lord (Luke 1:17). It is putting in order, arranging, so that everything is ready to receive or welcome.
3. When speaking of a way, it means to smooth it out, arrange it so that the road is passable (Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2, Luke 7:27). The image is that of a messenger going ahead to remove stones, fill in ditches, making the passage possible.
G2680.origine: The Greek word κατασκευάζω (kataskeuazō) is formed from the prefix κατα (kata-, "down, completely") and the verb σκευάζω (skeuazō, "to arrange, to equip"). The basic idea is to arrange the elements in an organized and complete manner. The word often translates the Hebrew בָּרָא (bara), which means "to create" or "to form." The root suggests the action of putting in place, structuring, making something functional and orderly.
G2680.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Hebrews. It is used to construct buildings (the house in Hebrews 3:3-4, the tent of worship in Hebrews 9:2) or to prepare what will be received (a people in Luke 1:17). But the dominant context is that of the way: John the Baptist is sent to prepare the way before Jesus (Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2, Luke 7:27), which means smoothing out spiritual and moral obstacles. The nuance thus changes according to the context: material construction for buildings, moral or spiritual preparation for people and paths.
G2680.portee: This word reminds us that the presentation of Jesus is not an isolated event, but the result of intentional preparation by God. John the Baptist "prepares the way": he removes the obstacles of the heart, he exhorts to repentance. For the Christian, this means that our hearts need to be "arranged" to receive the Lord. The word also invites us to see God's faithfulness: He builds His work with intention and order, nothing is left to chance.

sens: To settle somewhere by remaining
To perch, nest (for birds)
To rest, find shelter
To reside, live in a lasting way
G2681.detail:
1. The basic meaning is to settle somewhere in order to remain — it is the idea of establishing one's dwelling, one's daily life somewhere. This implies a certain stability and appropriation of the place.

2. For birds and creatures, it means to nest or perch: to find shelter, a place to settle and stay. In the three parables of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:32, Mark 4:32, Luke 13:19), the birds of the air come to dwell in the branches of the grown tree — the tree offers them a natural home.

3. The word can also mean to rest, to find refuge: in Acts 2:26, speaking of the resurrection, it says that the flesh will rest with hope, meaning it will find a lasting rest, a definitive dwelling.

4. Overall, to dwell always evokes the idea of a presence that establishes itself, takes place, and remains — whether it is a person settling in, a creature nesting, or a hope resting in the heart.
G2681.origine: The Greek word κατασκηνόω is composed of κατά ("down, over") and σκηνόω ("to pitch a tent, camp"), which itself comes from σκηνή ("tent"). The primary image is that of pitching one's tent, establishing a dwelling — hence to dwell, to reside. In Hebrew, the word סָכַךְ (sākak) often conveys the idea of covering or finding refuge, which explains why the Greek word applies to both birds finding shelter in the branches.
G2681.emploi: The verb κατασκηνόω appears 4 times in the New Testament, always with the same nuance: to dwell, to settle. Three occurrences are in the parallel parables of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:32, Mark 4:32, Luke 13:19): it describes how, when the tree has grown, the birds of the air come to dwell in its branches, finding lodging and protection there. The fourth occurrence in Acts 2:26 slightly deviates: it speaks of the flesh that will rest (or dwell) with hope at the resurrection — it is the idea of finding a lasting rest, a definitive dwelling. In all cases, the word implies a stable presence and an appropriation of the place.
G2681.portee: This word reminds us that God calls His children to find in Him a place of true rest. Just as the birds find shelter in the branches of the grown tree, we are invited to settle, to dwell in trust in Christ. The mention of the flesh that will rest with hope also opens a perspective of resurrection and eternal life: our definitive dwelling is not in this unstable world, but in God.

sens: The place where a bird settles and rests
The shelter, the refuge, the lodging of a creature
Figuratively, the home, the stable dwelling of a person
G2682.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the nest where birds settle and sleep: it is their natural place of rest and security. In Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58, Jesus says that "the birds of the air have nests" — each bird has its little shelter built or found to rest in.

2. More broadly, it refers to any lodging or shelter, a place where a living creature settles and takes refuge. The word conveys the idea of having a place to lay one's head, where to find rest and a certain stability.

3. Applied to humans, it evokes the home, the house, everything that allows us to have roots somewhere. When Jesus says, "the Son of Man has no nest," He emphasizes His voluntary destitution: unlike foxes and birds, He has nowhere to lay His head — not even a home to retreat to.
G2682.origine: The Greek word κατασκήνωσις (kataskēnōsis) comes from κατά (kata, "down, near") and σκήνη (skénè, "tent, dwelling"). It literally means "to settle under a tent," hence "to take quarters, to settle in." In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it translates the Hebrew מִשְׁכָּן (mishkan, "tabernacle") and other Hebrew terms designating habitation or dwelling. The Greek word evokes the image of a military camp or a temporary installation.
G2682.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the same saying of Jesus reported by Matthew and Luke. In Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58, Jesus contrasts the fate of animals — even foxes have dens, birds have nests — with His own condition as a wandering messenger without a fixed place of residence. The context is that of the call to the disciple who wants to follow Him: Jesus reminds him that life with Him involves renouncing material securities. It is a rare word, almost hapax, which highlights through its singular character the originality and weight of this statement.
G2682.portee: This verse reveals the real humanity and voluntary destitution of Jesus. He did not come to establish an earthly empire or a stable dwelling, but to live in poverty and mobility in service of His mission. For the disciple, it is a call to accept that following Jesus may require renouncing ordinary comforts and domestic securities. It also invites reflection on what truly constitutes a "home": not a building, but belonging and trust in God.

sens: To extend one's shadow over something to protect or hide it
To dominate or overshadow by one's imposing presence
G2683.detail:
1. To cover with one's shadow means to extend one's protective shadow over a person or thing. It is the image of the cherubim who, above the ark of the covenant, spread their wings to cover with their shadow the mercy seat, the seat of God's mercy (Hebrews 9:5). This shadow is not one that frightens, but one that protects and sanctifies.
2. The word also evokes a domination or an imposing presence that overshadows. When something covers you with its shadow, it can mean that this reality is so great, so present, that it dominates everything beneath it.
G2683.origine: The Greek word κατασκιάζω (kataskiazō) comes from the preposition κατα (kata), which marks the idea of what goes down or covers, and the verb σκιάζω (skiazō), which means "to cast a shadow" or "to shade." The root σκια (skia) designates the shadow itself. It is a rare verb, forged to express the divine action of covering and protecting through an invisible but real presence.
G2683.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:5, where it describes how the cherubim of glory cover with their shadow the mercy seat in the sanctuary of the old covenant. The author of the epistle uses it to express the idea that the presence of the angels is not only visible, but radiates a holiness that covers the most sacred place of Israelite worship.
G2683.portee: This verb reminds us that God manifests His protection and holiness through visible signs: the shadow of the cherubim over the ark symbolizes how divine glory envelops the very heart of worship. For the believer today, it invites us to recognize that God is never far away, that His presence covers us, even when it remains invisible to the eyes.

sens: to secretly observe someone to monitor or denounce them
to examine closely to discover
to look closely to judge or criticize
G2684.detail:
1. To spy means to observe someone in secret, often to trap or control them. In Galatians 2:4, Paul speaks of false brothers who had sneaked into the assembly to spy on the freedom of believers in Jesus Christ — that is, to monitor how Christians lived out this freedom, with the intention of enslaving them to the Law.
2. The word can also mean to examine closely, to look very carefully to inspect or discover something hidden. It is a meticulous and intentional observation.
3. In some contexts, to spy also carries the idea of observing to judge or criticize, particularly to detect failures or infractions.
G2684.origine: The Greek word κατασκοπέω (kataskopeō) is composed of κατά (kata), which means "down" or "through," and σκοπέω (skopéō), "to look" or "to examine." Together, they form the idea of looking attentively, of scrutiny or inspection. The root σκοπ- (skop-) evokes a gaze directed with intensity. In Hebrew, the word רָגַל (ragal) meaning "to explore" or "to spy" in the background expresses the same intentional surveillance.
G2684.emploi: This Greek verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 2:4. Paul uses it to describe the action of false brothers who had infiltrated the Christian assembly. These intruders were not merely seeking to observe: they aimed to examine and monitor how Christians exercised their freedom in Christ, in order to find a pretext to reduce them to the slavery of the Mosaic Law. The context shows that the spying had a hostile and manipulative intent. It is a gaze that seeks not to understand, but to accuse and control.
G2684.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that there are always forces seeking to surveil and restrict the freedom that Christ has won for us. Paul warns us against those who, seemingly close, actually aim to bring us back under the yoke of legalistic rules. Understanding this term helps us remain vigilant against those who, under the pretext of faith or tradition, attempt to take away the freedom of the Spirit.

sens: a person sent secretly to observe and report
one who sneaks in to spy
hidden informant
G2685.detail:
1. A spy is someone sent secretly to a place to observe, listen, and learn information that they will report back to the one who dispatched them. They are a hidden observer, a trusted envoy tasked with seeing without being seen. In Hebrews 11:31, Rahab receives the spies that Joshua sent to scout the city of Jericho: these men come to secretly assess the defenses and strength of the enemy.
2. By extension, the word refers to anyone who sneaks somewhere in secret, concealing their true role or purpose, to observe or listen to what is happening.
G2685.origine: The Greek word κατάσκοπος comes from κατά ("against," "toward") and σκοπέω ("to look," "to observe"). It literally means an "observer who looks toward, who aims." The root "skopéo" evokes the action of fixing one's gaze with attention, hence the French "scope" (sight). The Hebrew word רָגַל (ragal, "foot") conveys the idea of one who walks in secret, one who advances stealthily, illustrating how we speak of spies: people who move quietly.
G2685.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:31. It is in the context of the spies that Joshua secretly sends to Jericho before the assault, to inform the Israelites about the city. Rahab, although she is a prostitute and a foreigner, shows her faith by receiving these men kindly instead of denouncing them to her king. This act of trust and protection towards the spies becomes for the author of the epistle a remarkable example of true faith, worthy of being mentioned alongside Abraham and Moses.
G2685.portee: The story of Rahab and the spies teaches that true faith is manifested through concrete and courageous actions, even when one risks everything. Rahab does not know the God of Israel, but she believes in His promise and acts accordingly. This example reminds us that God honors sincere faith, no matter who we are or where we come from, and that a simple act of hospitality and trust can place us on God's side in His plans.

sens: To act with cunning and malice towards someone to deceive or dominate them
To resort to schemes to harm
To deploy intelligent malice
G2686.detail: 1. To act with cunning and malice towards someone to deceive or dominate them: this means using indirect strategies, calculated maneuvers to gain an advantage over an opponent. In Acts 7:19, Pharaoh "uses cunning" against the Israelites: he employs crafty reasoning and schemes to justify oppression and infanticide, acting with perverse intelligence. 2. To resort to schemes to harm: the word depicts someone who thinks and plans maliciously. Pharaoh does not persecute merely as a brutal tyrant, but combines calculation and malice. 3. To deploy intelligent malice: it is the cunning of the wicked who believes themselves wise, who disguises their crimes as politics or state reasons.
G2686.origine: The word comes from the Greek "sophos" (wise, shrewd) preceded by the prefix "kata" (against, upon). The basic image is thus that of a "wisdom" turned against someone, an intelligence used for evil. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew "hakam" in the reflexive form, which means "to show oneself wise" but here "to act with cunning." It is a corrupted wisdom, perverted into malice.
G2686.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:19, in Stephen's speech. It specifically refers to the conduct of the Pharaoh of Egypt who, seeing the multiplication of the Israelites, invents intelligent pretexts to enslave them and attempt to destroy their descendants. This passage shows how the word applies to a person in power who abuses their authority not through simple brutality, but through calculated cunning, often hidden under a veneer of political rationality.
G2686.portee: This word reminds the believer that human malice is not limited to brute violence, but can wear the mask of wisdom. It invites discernment of the sly strategies that oppress the innocent, and to recognize that even earthly power cannot escape God's judgment, who sees beyond the artifices of men.

sens: Calm an agitation, an angry crowd
Master a movement, an emotion that is too intense
G2687.detail:
1. To appease a crowd means to reduce its agitation and anger to bring it back to calm. The town clerk of Ephesus, faced with the crowd gathered in the theater shouting in favor of the goddess Diana, calms the spirits by inviting them to be silent and listen (Acts 19:35). The image is that of someone who "brings down" the tumultuous energy of a group.
2. To master means to hold back, to restrain a reaction, a passion that threatens to get out of control. The clerk asks the crowd to calm down and not to act hastily (Acts 19:36): it is about dominating the impulse to act wisely. It is to contain a force that could cause disorder.
G2687.origine: The Greek word is composed of the preposition "kata" (down, against) and the verb "stellō" (arrange, dispose, set). The basic image is that of "bringing down," of lowering something that is rising or agitated. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb also translates Hebrew words concerning restraint and inner calm.
G2687.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same scene (Acts 19). It is a crisis situation: a large crowd is gathered in the theater of Ephesus, very excited, shouting and descending into violence to defend the worship of Diana threatened by Paul's preaching. The town clerk first intervenes to appease the agitated crowd (Acts 19:35), then the crowd itself must calm down to avoid acting under the influence of passion (Acts 19:36). The verb thus evokes both the action of someone intervening from the outside to restore order and the effort of someone who must master their own reactions.
G2687.portee: This word teaches us that calm and reason must prevail over emotional agitation, even when we believe we are defending something important. It is a lesson for disciples: in the face of threats or challenges, calmness and reflection are better than panic or violence. It also invites us to recognize the role of one who, with authority or wisdom, knows how to restore order in chaos.

sens: the physical demeanor of a person, their way of standing and presenting themselves
the overall appearance, the external aspect, what is immediately visible
the moral and spiritual bearing that shines through behavior and presence
G2688.detail:
1. The word first designates how someone "holds" their body and shows themselves physically. It is the bearing, the presence, the way one carries oneself and presents oneself to others. In Titus 2:3, Paul asks older women for an "appearance" (the word used in the Segond) that is suitable for holiness: a demeanor, a visible dignity.
2. It is also about the overall appearance, what one sees and perceives about a person even before they speak. This external aspect is the first testimony that one bears.
3. For Paul, this physical bearing reveals an inner condition: an older woman must have a bearing "worthy of holiness" because her very presence must reflect her attachment to God. Bearing is never separated from the heart.
G2688.origine: The word comes from the root "καθίστημι" (cathístēmi), which means "establish, constitute, place." Bearing is thus what "establishes" or "places" you in the presence of others — your way of being "constituted" and established. It is a notion of posture in a broad sense: not only how you stand, but in what state you present yourself.
G2688.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:3. Paul uses it to instruct Titus on the conduct that older women ("presbytides") should have. He asks that they have a bearing, a demeanor that is in accordance with holiness. What stands out is that physical and moral bearing are not separated: Paul is not only talking about clothing, but about the overall way of presenting and holding oneself, which must reflect a life devoted to God.
G2688.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith is not hidden or invisible. Our way of standing, our presence, our overall bearing — what we call our "bearing" — testifies to what we believe and live. Paul tells older women that their bearing must be worthy of holiness: this means that others, upon seeing them, should perceive something of the dignity and respect we owe to God. It is a call to authenticity: not a feigned appearance, but a presence where the inside and outside are in harmony.

sens: A measured and appropriate appearance in clothing
An attitude of restraint and tranquility in behavior
The demeanor or external presentation of a person
G2689.detail:
1. The word first designates a simple and honest appearance in clothing, without excess or ostentation — this is what pleases God when a woman dresses modestly (1 Timothy 2:9).
2. Beyond clothing, it is an inner attitude that manifests outwardly: a form of calm, restraint, and moral stability in the way one presents and holds oneself.
3. The word can also simply evoke a garment or attire, that is, everything that clothes or adorns us, taken in the sense of overall appearance.
G2689.origine: The word comes from the verb that means "to bring down," "to stop," "to restrain" — the idea is one of reduction, of a measure imposed. Literally, it is something that "holds back" or "masters" the appearance, that "keeps it in place." That is why it has taken on the meaning of "appropriate clothing" (what adorns us with measure) and of "composed behavior." In Hebrew, the word that the Septuagint uses for this term refers to a veil or a garment of modesty.
G2689.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:9, where Paul recommends to women a "modest manner" of dressing — not elaborate braids, nor gold or pearl ornaments, nor expensive clothes, but a simple and modest presentation. It is a rare term, but its meaning is clear: it is about an attire that reflects sobriety, modesty, and self-respect, qualities that Paul values in women who want to serve the Church faithfully. The derived adjective will also be used to describe reserved and orderly behavior.
G2689.portee: This word invites Christians to consider their external appearance not as a means of seduction or display, but as an expression of inner wisdom and the respect one owes to oneself and to others. It is a call to sobriety and restraint, not out of guilt, but because true beauty comes from a tranquil and faithful soul. This exhortation aligns with the biblical teaching that our body is the temple of the Holy Spirit and deserves to be presented with honor.

sens: To turn downwards, to return (the soil, the earth)
To overturn, to topple (a table, a structure)
To destroy, to annihilate (a city, a system)
G2690.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical and concrete: to turn something downwards, as one turns the soil of the ground to cultivate or loosen it.
2. The word is also used to refer to overturning objects: Jesus overturned the tables of the money changers in the temple (Matthew 21:12), a violent and symbolic gesture of expulsion. It is to topple something that was upright or established.
3. In a figurative sense, the word can refer to the destruction of a larger entity: to overturn a city, a house, or even an established order — the complete annihilation of a structure.
G2690.origine: The word is composed of κατα- ("downwards," marking completion or intensity) and στρέφω ("to turn, to return"). The basic image is that of rotation downwards. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates it with הָפַךְ ("to overturn, to return"), which carries a very similar idea: a movement that causes something to topple over.
G2690.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Gospel, in parallel accounts of the cleansing of the temple: Matthew 21:12 and Mark 11:15. In both passages, Jesus overturns the tables of the money changers and the sellers of pigeons — a dramatic act of purification of the holy place. It is a word of strong action, emphasizing the prophetic violence of Christ's gesture against the commercial desecration of the temple.
G2690.portee: The overturning of the tables by Jesus reminds us that God does not accept the compromise of true worship by unjust or selfish practices. This verb illustrates how divine justice can intervene forcefully to restore order and holiness, inviting the believer not to ignore the mixture between authentic faith and human interests.

sens: To be drawn away from something by carnal desire
To be dominated by pleasure to the detriment of one's commitments
To abandon one's principles or fidelity under the influence of carnal pleasures
G2691.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of being led away from a position or commitment by bodily desires. A young widow seeking to remarry, Paul says, is "detached from Christ" by pleasure — she allows herself to be drawn towards other concerns (1 Timothy 5:11).

2. The image is that of a person who, because of the growing sensuality within them, gradually moves away from what should be their priority: their devotion to God and their past commitment. It is not a one-time act, but a slow process of seduction by carnal pleasures.

3. The word carries a judgment: it is not only about desiring something carnal, but about being dominated by that desire to the point of abandoning more serious vows or promises. It is pleasure that takes the reins and diverts the person from their path.
G2691.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "kata" (downwards, against) and "streniaô" (to indulge in debauchery, to enjoy carnal pleasures). This root evokes the idea of letting oneself go, of relaxing into pleasure. The prefix "kata" gives the verb a nuance of intensity or movement downwards — one does not simply enjoy, one is dominated, one collapses under the weight of desire. It is a rare verb in Greek, emphasizing the seriousness of this diversion.
G2691.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 5:11. Paul speaks of young widows who wish to remarry. He says they are "detached from Christ" by pleasure — carnal desire has gradually led them away from their initial commitment to remain widows to serve the Lord. This context shows that Paul does not condemn marriage itself, but the inconsistency and abandonment of promises under the pressure of carnal desires. The word designates an inner process where sensuality gains ground and weakens fidelity.
G2691.portee: This word reminds the reader of the spiritual reality often hidden behind human choices: our carnal desires, if not mastered, can gradually lead us away from our commitment to God and our promises. Paul does not harshly accuse these young widows, but invites vigilance — pleasure is a power that works silently and diverts our hearts. It is a call to keep our spiritual priorities above our inclinations.

sens: Physical destruction, complete upheaval of a city or place
Moral or spiritual reversal, fall into evil
Damage caused to a person's faith or convictions
G2692.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes physical destruction, the violent overturning of a city or a structure: in 2 Peter 2:6, it refers to the destruction of the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, reduced to ashes as a warning to the ungodly. 2. In a figurative sense, it refers to the overturning of principles, the collapse of what was established: in 2 Timothy 2:14, the disputes over words that only serve to ruin those who listen, meaning to make them fall, to mislead them in their convictions. 3. Thus, it is a spiritual damage: something that destroys the moral solidity or certainty of faith in the one who is affected.
G2692.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to overturn, to destroy from above downwards": the prefix "kata" reinforces this idea of a collapse that goes from top to bottom. It is the image of something collapsing, falling in on itself. The word is used to translate the Hebrew "destruction, calamity" from the Old Testament into Greek.
G2692.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 2 Peter 2:6, it describes a real and visible event: the destruction of ancient cities. In 2 Timothy 2:14, it denotes an invisible yet real collapse: that of convictions and faith in the believer. In both cases, it is something serious and irreversible.
G2692.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that there are words and activities — like sterile disputes — that do not build faith but undermine it. It is a call to choose conversations and behaviors that edify rather than destroy. Ruin is never far for one who strays from the solidity of truth.

sens: To be laid low, to be brought down
To be annihilated, to disappear
G2693.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of being thrown to the ground, laid low — it is the idea of physical destruction or annihilation. In 1 Corinthians 10:5, Paul recounts that most of the Israelites in the desert "perished": they were struck down, eliminated, their bodies lay in the desert according to the account in Numbers.
2. In a figurative sense, "to perish" means to be annihilated, to disappear, to no longer exist or count. It is death striking, definitive elimination. The biblical example shows that this destruction was not accidental: it came from God, who found these Israelites displeasing.
G2693.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "kata" (downwards, against) and the verb "strōnnumi" (to spread out, to lay down). The basic image is that of laying something low, spreading it on the ground — hence the meaning of throwing down, striking down. In Hebrew, this Greek word translates terms like "chatal" (to strike, to massacre) or "chataḥ" (to spread out, to strike down), which share this same idea of brutal destruction and annihilation.
G2693.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 10:5, where Paul uses it to describe the fate of the Israelites in the desert. He relies on the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) to emphasize that most of them "perished" — in other words, were struck down and eliminated by God's judgment — even though they all benefited from the same spiritual favors (the cloud, the crossing of the sea, the manna). It is a word of destruction or divine punishment.
G2693.portee: Paul cites this event in the desert to warn the Corinthians: those who enjoy God's blessings are not automatically safe from judgment. If most of the Israelites perished despite the miracles they witnessed, Christians must guard against idolatry and unfaithfulness. This word reminds us that grace is not a guarantee, but a responsibility.

sens: To pull someone forcefully down or forward
To bring someone against their will before an authority
G2694.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a physical action: to drag someone means to pull them with force, as one would drag a heavy object across the ground. The image evokes violence, brutality — one does not drag someone who consents.
2. In its only biblical usage (Luke 12:58), the word describes a concrete and dramatic situation: a creditor dragging his debtor before the judge. It is an image of the urgency of forgiveness: it is better to reconcile quickly than to be dragged forcefully before the court, for once there, you will have no escape.
G2694.origine: The word is composed of the prefix κατα (which indicates intensity or downward movement) and the verb σύρω (to drag). It thus expresses the idea of dragging intensely, with force. The root σύρ- evokes dragging, sliding. The word appears rarely in the New Testament: it is present in the Greek Old Testament with Hebrew verbs expressing a force that devastates or carries away (such as חָשַׂף, "to strip," or שָׁטַף, "to flood").
G2694.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Luke 12:58. Jesus uses it in a parable about reconciliation: he urges his disciples to resolve their disputes quickly before they find themselves in court. The word paints the worst-case scenario — being dragged by a creditor or an adversary to the tribunal — to motivate immediate action. It is a striking and concrete image of what happens if one postpones forgiveness.
G2694.portee: This word from Jesus teaches the urgency of forgiveness and reconciliation. Waiting, dragging one's feet in a dispute, risks being dragged against one's will before a judge, where all control is lost. It invites the believer to act quickly, to seek peace rather than let resentment build up.

sens: To take life violently and brutally
To eliminate ruthlessly opponents or enemies
G2695.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of killing, taking life through violence. The basic image evokes a brutal execution, without mercy. In the parable of the talents in Luke 19:27, the king orders to kill ("kill") his political enemies in his presence: it is the violent execution of those who have rebelled against him.
2. It is also used in a figurative sense to eliminate or completely annihilate. In this parable context, the verb carries a strong emotional charge: it expresses relentlessness, implacability in the face of insubordination.
G2695.origine: The word is composed of the Greek prefix "kata-" (downward, against) and the verb "sphazô" (to slaughter, to cut). This root evokes the very concrete image of an animal being slaughtered or brought down. The prefix intensifies the idea: not just to kill, but to kill definitively, resolutely. In ancient Hebrew, the same meaning is conveyed by words like "hârag" (to kill, to strike fatally).
G2695.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:27. It occurs in the conclusion of the parable of the minas, where a king settles accounts with his servants. Those who have rejected his authority are doomed to destruction. The use of the compound verb "katasphazô" rather than a simple "to kill" emphasizes the determination and ruthlessness of the judgment. It is a strong term that marks an irreversible break.
G2695.portee: This parable speaks of the final judgment and the fate reserved for those who reject Christ's authority. The verb "to kill" is not an incitement to violence, but an image of divine judgment without appeal. It invites the disciple to recognize the seriousness of the consequences of rejecting Christ and the reality of the coming judgment.

sens: To close or mark something with a seal for security or authentication
To render hermetically closed and guaranteed
Figuratively: to make inviolable or secret
G2696.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to close and secure something by applying a seal — an official stamp or distinctive mark. In Revelation 5:1, the book is sealed with seven seals, meaning it is closed by several successive marks that protect and authenticate it, and that no one can open it until these seals are lifted.
2. To seal can also mean to make something hermetically closed, so that it cannot be opened or accessed: it is the image of the seal applied to soft wax that hardens and locks everything.
3. Figuratively, to seal expresses the idea of making something inviolable, secret, or reserved for the one who has the authority to open it. In the apocalyptic context, the seven seals guard the secret of destiny and the will of God until the appointed time.
G2696.origine: The Greek word κατασφραγίζω (katasphragizō) is formed from κατα (kata, "completely") and σφραγίζω (sphragizō, "to seal"). The root σφραγίς (sphragis) refers to the seal itself, the tool or mark. It is an image from ancient daily life: all official documents, letters, contracts were closed with a wax seal bearing the signer's imprint to guarantee authenticity and prevent alteration en route. The Hebrew word חָתַם (hatam), "to seal," carries the same concrete idea.
G2696.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 5:1. In this passage, John sees the divine book in the hand of the one who is on the throne, and this book is sealed with seven seals. This central image reveals that the fate of the world and the fulfillment of divine plans are closed, kept secret, until the Lamb (Jesus) is worthy and able to open them one by one. The seals mark both protection, authenticity, and the mystery of God's project.
G2696.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on God's sovereignty and secrecy. As long as the seals are not broken, no one can access the content of the divine plan; it is a call to trust and patience in waiting for fulfillment. The image of the seal also speaks of authenticity: only the one who has the right to open can do so, which underscores the absolute authority of the risen Christ in the history of salvation.

sens: the act of holding something firmly, keeping it under control
territory or property over which one has control and enjoyment
inheritance passed down and preserved by a family
G2697.detail:
1. The word κατάσχεσις primarily denotes the action of holding firmly, maintaining under one's authority. It is the gesture of one who grips something or keeps it in mastery: in Acts 7:5, God promises Abraham a possession, meaning a territory that he will hold and from which his descendants will benefit.
2. In Acts 7:45, the word applies to the land that the Israelites received and occupied after crossing the desert: it is the concrete territory they take control of and inhabit, driving out the nations that were there.
3. The underlying idea is that of an acquired and preserved good, often passed down from generation to generation: what one possesses solidly, what becomes heritage.
G2697.origine: The word comes from the verb κατέχω, which means "to hold," "to retain," "to maintain firmly." The prefix κατά reinforces the idea of total control. In the Greek Old Testament, κατάσχεσις almost always translates the Hebrew אֲחֻזָּה (aḥuzza), which denotes a possession, a property, especially that which is held firmly or passed on to heirs.
G2697.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 7, in Stephen's speech. In Acts 7:5, it refers to the promise made by God to Abraham: although Abraham owned no land at the time of the promise, God commits to giving him possession and making his descendants inherit it. In Acts 7:45, Stephen applies the same word to the land entered into possession by Israel after the Exodus. In both cases, κατάσχεσις emphasizes stable and lasting control, a good that one holds and can transmit.
G2697.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's promises are not vague: what He promises, He gives to hold firmly. For Abraham as for Israel, the promised possession was not a dream, but a reality inscribed in God's plan. It also invites the reader to perceive spiritual inheritance as something solid and transmissible: a true possession, not just a suspended hope.

sens: to do good to someone, to be pleasing to them
to deliberately seek to win someone's favor
to accumulate for personal gain
G2698.detail: 1. The fundamental meaning is that of "to accumulate" or "to store up" — the prefix κατα (kata) reinforces the idea of "depositing." In classical Greek, one would speak of "depositing" a sum of money or "setting aside" for later. In the two passages in Acts that use this word, it has shifted to a figurative sense: it refers to accumulating favor or goodwill with someone. 2. "To please" here conveys the idea of actively seeking to win someone over, to "store up" their sympathy. Felix and Festus aim for one thing: to win the favor of the Jews (Acts 24:27 and 25:9). It is a voluntary, almost calculated act — one wonders what they expect to gain from it.
G2698.origine: The word combines κατα (kata, "down, completely") and τίθημι (tithēmi, "to place, to put"). Its basic image is thus that of a deposit, of storing up. In Hebrew, the Septuagint translates this verb for words like שׁוּב (shoûv, "to turn") or יָצַק (yatsaq, "to pour"), but Greek has chosen this image of accumulation to also express the idea of gaining or deserving something.
G2698.emploi: The Greek word κατατίθημι appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the book of Acts. In Acts 24:27, Felix hopes to please the Jews by keeping Paul in prison. In Acts 25:9, Festus seeks to please the Jews by proposing to go up to Jerusalem. In both cases, these are Roman magistrates calculating their politics to maintain the favor of a population. The verb carries a slightly pejorative nuance: these leaders are not seeking what is right, but what will gain them influential friends.
G2698.portee: This word reminds the reader of the dangers of conformity and the pursuit of popularity. Felix and Festus forget justice in order to "please" — that is, to build up a capital of sympathy. Paul, on the other hand, does not seek to please his human judges. The verb invites every Christian to examine their motives: do we act out of justice and faithfulness, or out of a calculation of popularity?

sens: Mutilation, incision of the body
Counterfeit of true circumcision
Judaism without the faith of the heart
G2699.detail:
1. The word literally refers to an incision or mutilation of the body — the act of cutting or slicing the flesh. This is the primary meaning, which refers to the wounds that idolaters inflicted upon themselves in certain pagan cults or which the Law prohibited Levite priests from marking on their bodies (Leviticus 21:5).
2. In Philippians 3:2, Paul uses this word sarcastically to refer to the circumcision of the Judaizers — those Christians who demanded obedience to the Mosaic Law and physical circumcision for salvation. The play on words is brutal: instead of saying "circumcision" ("περιτομή"), Paul says "mutilation" — a true incision of the flesh, but devoid of meaning since it no longer rests on faith in Christ.
3. Ultimately, this word reveals that true circumcision is not a physical mark, but a work of the heart. The false circumcised maintain the external gesture without the spiritual reality.
G2699.origine: The word is composed of "κατα" (down, indicating intensity) and "τομή" (the cut, the section). It concretely refers to the act of cutting or incising. The root "τέμνω" (to cut) also appears in other Greek words related to wounds or incisions. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew words designating prohibited mutilations — such as "שׁרט" (to cut oneself) — cover roughly the same domain.
G2699.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:2. Paul uses it to mock the Judaizers who harassed the Church of Philippi by imposing circumcision as a condition for salvation. He refuses to call them "circumcised" (the honorable term): he calls them "false circumcised," reducing their practice to mere mutilation of the flesh. It is a combative, polemical word that shows how Paul viewed this legalistic demand as a perversion of the true mystery of the circumcision of the heart in Christ.
G2699.portee: This word reminds Christians that true relationship with God is never a matter of external marks or legalistic conformity. Paul invites the Church here to remain vigilant: those who reduce faith to carnal rules and visible signs distance themselves from the spiritual reality of Christ. It is an invitation to seek substance rather than appearance.
